questions.stem: Which of the following best defines inflation?

options.option_text: A one-time increase in the price of a single commodity
A sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services in an economy
A decrease in the production of goods
An increase in the nominal value of currency

questions.explanation: Inflation is a SUSTAINED rise in the GENERAL price level — not a one-off change or a sectoral change. It erodes the purchasing power of money: the same rupee buys fewer goods over time. Measured via indices like CPI and WPI. A single commodity's price rise (e.g., tomatoes in monsoon) is NOT inflation if average prices are stable. An increase in nominal currency value is the opposite (deflation/currency strengthening).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In India, which of the following is the primary inflation index used by the RBI for its monetary policy decisions?
questions.explanation: Since 2014 (Urjit Patel Committee + 2016 Monetary Policy Framework Agreement), the RBI targets HEADLINE CPI-Combined (released by NSO/MoSPI) with a central target of 4% ± 2%. WPI (Office of Economic Adviser, DPIIT) is used for deflating GDP at constant prices and tracking producer prices, but NOT as the RBI's policy target. CPI-IW (Labour Bureau) is used for DA calculations for govt employees, not RBI targeting.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of 'cost-push' inflation?

options.option_text: A boom in consumer demand during a festival
A sharp increase in crude oil prices raising transport and production costs

questions.explanation: COST-PUSH inflation arises when input costs (raw materials, wages, fuel) rise and producers pass this on to consumers. Classic example: oil shocks (1973 OPEC crisis, 2008 oil spike). DEMAND-PULL inflation arises when aggregate demand exceeds supply (option A — festival demand surge). Excess money printing is typically classified as demand-pull/monetary inflation (option C). A stock rally is asset-price inflation, not general inflation.

questions.stem: What is the current inflation target band set for the RBI under the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement?
questions.explanation: The RBI's flexible inflation targeting framework sets a MEDIUM-TERM target of 4% CPI-Combined, with a tolerance band of ±2 percentage points (lower bound 2%, upper bound 6%). This was first set in 2016 (initial 5-year review) and was retained at the March 2021 review for another 5 years (2021-26). If inflation breaches the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the government explaining reasons and remedial actions.

questions.stem: Galloping inflation refers to inflation of:
questions.explanation: Inflation categories: (1) Creeping/Mild — <3%; (2) Walking/Trotting — 3-10%; (3) GALLOPING/Running — 10-1000%; (4) Hyperinflation — >1000% per year (e.g., Weimar Germany 1923, Zimbabwe 2008, Venezuela 2018). Galloping inflation disrupts business planning and wage contracts. Deflation is NEGATIVE inflation (falling prices) and is generally considered a warning sign of slump.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a MONETARY POLICY tool that the RBI uses to control inflation?

options.option_text: Raising or lowering Income Tax rates

questions.explanation: MONETARY policy tools are used by the CENTRAL BANK (RBI). Key tools: Repo Rate, Reverse Repo Rate, MSF, Bank Rate, CRR, SLR, OMO (Open Market Operations). Changing Repo Rate (lending rate for banks to RBI) influences bank interest rates → consumer borrowing/saving → aggregate demand → inflation. Income Tax is a FISCAL POLICY tool (Finance Ministry). Government bonds are fiscal. MSP is set by Cabinet on CACP recommendation — neither monetary nor a direct fiscal tool.

options.option_text: Low/stagnant growth accompanied by high inflation and unemployment
Stable prices combined with zero unemployment

questions.explanation: STAGFLATION = STAGnation + inFLATION. It is the coexistence of (1) slow/zero economic growth, (2) high inflation, and (3) elevated unemployment. It challenges the classical Phillips-curve view that inflation and unemployment trade off. Famous example: US in 1970s during oil shocks. Policymakers face a dilemma: tightening money controls inflation but worsens unemployment; loosening controls does the opposite.

questions.stem: The business cycle typically consists of four phases. Which phase is characterized by declining output, rising unemployment, and falling prices?
questions.explanation: Business cycle phases: (1) EXPANSION — GDP rising, employment up, prices rising modestly; (2) PEAK — growth at maximum, economy overheated; (3) CONTRACTION/RECESSION — GDP falling, unemployment rising, prices falling or rising slowly; (4) TROUGH — economy at its bottom before recovery. A recession is technically defined as TWO consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth (NBER uses broader criteria). Great Depression (1929-33) was a severe contraction.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes 'core inflation'?

options.option_text: Inflation in all goods and services
Inflation faced by rural consumers only

questions.explanation: CORE INFLATION strips out volatile items (food and fuel) from headline CPI to reveal underlying inflation trends driven by broader demand-supply conditions. Food/fuel are excluded because they swing due to monsoons, crude shocks, etc. — noise that obscures the inflation signal. Central banks watch core inflation closely since it responds more predictably to monetary policy. In India, core is often quoted alongside headline in RBI bi-monthly reviews. i.e., non-volatile components.

questions.stem: Who chairs the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which decides the repo rate?
questions.explanation: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has 6 members: 3 from RBI (Governor, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one officer nominated by RBI Central Board) + 3 external members (nominated by the Government of India for 4-year terms). The RBI Governor CHAIRS the MPC and has a CASTING VOTE in case of a tie. The MPC meets at least 4 times a year (usually 6) and decisions are made by majority vote. The PM and FM have no direct vote.
